rounds.proof_sketch: Input shape = [16, 16384] → size = 16 * 16384 = 262144. Scalar kernel is only called when size < 1024. Since 262144 >= 1024, the code always takes the vectorized kernel branch. The mutation on line 48 is in hardsigmoid_kernel_scalar which is NEVER executed for this input size.
rounds.survival_reason: The mutation changes threadIdx.x to threadIdx.y in the scalar kernel (hardsigmoid_kernel_scalar). However, the dispatch logic uses the scalar kernel only when size < 1024. For the fixed input shape [16, 16384], size = 262144 which is far greater than 1024, so the vectorized kernel (hardsigmoid_kernel_vectorized) is always selected. The vectorized kernel is identical between original and mutant. Since the mutated code path is never executed, no value-level input can distinguish the mutant from the original under this fixed-shape contract.
rounds.kill_strategy: Unkillable under fixed-shape contract. The mutation resides in the scalar kernel which is only invoked for tensors with fewer than 1024 elements. The fixed input specification requires shape [16, 16384] with 262144 elements, guaranteeing the vectorized kernel is always used. Killing this mutant would require changing the tensor shape to have fewer than 1024 total elements, which violates the testing contract.
rounds.recommendations: Mutation testing frameworks should track code coverage to identify mutations in unreachable code paths for the given input configuration. When kernel dispatch depends on input size thresholds (here: size >= 1024), test specifications should either (a) include sizes that exercise all branches, or (b) exclude mutations in branches unreachable for the contracted input shapes. Consider generating mutant-specific test inputs that probe the branch conditions leading to mutated code.
